passage: I'm Santosh, Yash's roommate in the hostel. For eight months he was with a girl from his course, and I liked her. But I noticed things. She laughed at his plan to join a rural health project after graduation and said he should aim for a "proper" job abroad. He stopped talking about it. Then one night in March he came back early, sat on his bed and didn't switch on the light. They'd broken up. For two weeks he skipped the mess and slept through lectures. I dragged him to the canteen for chai. He didn't say much. In April I saw him at the notice board, reading about the rural project again. He applied. He told me, "I think I'd stopped being myself with her."

qa.q: What project did Yash apply to in April?
qa.a: He applied to the rural health project.

qa.q: What does Yash's line "I'd stopped being myself with her" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he realised that their values clashed and that he had been hiding his own goals to keep the relationship.

qa.q: How did Santosh help Yash during the hard weeks?
qa.a: He didn't lecture or pry, but kept him connected by dragging him out for chai, which gave Yash quiet company while he recovered.

qa.q: How might Yash's ex-girlfriend see the breakup?
qa.a: She may see it differently, perhaps feeling they wanted different lives, and be sad too, though the passage only shows Yash's side.

grounding: A roommate observes a young man recover from a breakup and realise his partner did not share his values.

passage:
Before: Neelam had liked Jaya from her college drama club for months. On a Monday, after rehearsal, she finally said it. Jaya smiled kindly and said, "I really like you as a friend, but not that way." Neelam laughed it off, then cried in the auto home.

During: For the next two weeks she avoided the club. She re-read old messages and felt stupid. On Saturday her cousin took her for a long walk and asked what she actually wanted in a partner. Neelam listed things: kindness, humour, someone who likes quiet evenings. "Jaya was all that," she said. "Then you know what to look for," her cousin said.

After: A month later, Neelam went back to drama. She and Jaya shared a scene. It stung a little, but less.

qa.q: What did Jaya say when Neelam told her how she felt?
qa.a: She said she really liked Neelam as a friend, but not that way.

qa.q: Why did Neelam re-read old messages and feel stupid?
qa.a: She was hurt by the rejection and embarrassed, wondering if she had misread Jaya's friendliness.

qa.q: How did the walk with her cousin help Neelam?
qa.a: Listing what she wanted in a partner turned the rejection into clarity about her own values, so it felt less like a personal failure.

qa.q: What is it like for Jaya to share a scene with Neelam afterwards?
qa.a: She may feel a bit awkward but relieved that Neelam returned, since she clearly cared about her as a friend.

grounding: It shows a young woman handling romantic rejection over several weeks and clarifying what she values in a partner.

passage: Sit, Sabina. You asked me how I knew your Phuphi's husband was the right one? Let me tell you about my friend Amandeep, before I tell you about me. She was engaged at twenty-one to a charming boy. Everyone loved him. But she noticed he never asked about her work at the library, and when she mentioned wanting to study further, he said, "After marriage you won't need to." It sat in her like a stone. She called off the engagement. Oh, the talk in the family! She cried for months. But three years later she met someone who helped her fill out her master's application. They're still married, still arguing about books. Charm is nice, beta. But look at what they want your life to be.

qa.q: Where did Amandeep work?
qa.a: She worked at the library.

qa.q: What does "It sat in her like a stone" suggest about Amandeep's feelings?
qa.a: It suggests his words left a heavy, lasting worry that his vision of her future clashed with what she valued.

qa.q: What advice does the elder give Sabina, and why is it wise?
qa.a: To look past charm and notice what a partner wants her life to be, because shared values matter more over time.

qa.q: How might Amandeep's family have seen her calling off the engagement?
qa.a: Many may have been shocked or disapproving at the time, but later they might understand why she did it.

passage:
Dear Zainab,
Thanks for listening last night. I know I talked in circles. Let me put it simply.
Raghav and I have been together five months. He's kind. But when things started getting physical, I felt rushed, and I froze instead of saying so. Nothing happened I didn't agree to, but I didn't like freezing.
So on Sunday I told him, calmly: I want to slow down, and I want us to talk before, not after. He was quiet, then said, "Thank you for telling me. I'd hate for you to feel that way."
We also agreed to go to the campus health centre together to talk about protection and testing, like adults.
I feel lighter. Also slightly embarrassed writing this. 😅
Usha

qa.q: Where did Usha and Raghav agree to go together?
qa.a: They agreed to go to the campus health centre.

qa.q: Why did Usha feel uneasy even though nothing happened without Usha's agreement?
qa.a: Usha froze instead of speaking up, so the boundary never got said, and that was unsettling.

qa.q: What made Usha's conversation with Raghav effective?
qa.a: Usha chose a calm moment, stated clearly what was needed, and they planned to get proper health information together.

qa.q: How might Raghav feel after Usha's honesty?
qa.a: He seemed grateful and caring, and may feel more trust in the relationship knowing Usha will tell him how things feel.

grounding: A young adult's letter shows Usha communicating boundaries and planning responsible sexual health care with a partner.

passage: You asked on the show what consent actually looks like in real life. I'm Varun, twenty. Honestly, I used to think it was just about no. Then something happened with my ex, and a friend, Ramesh, who'd trained as a peer educator, sat me down. He asked, "Did you check if she wanted it, or just that she didn't stop you?" That hit hard. I'd never thought about the difference. So now I ask. Out loud. Even when it feels awkward. "Is this okay?" "Want to stop?" And I've learned the answer can change halfway. Ramesh also pushed me to get tested and carry protection, and not treat that as someone else's job. It's less awkward than you'd think. Being unsure is way more awkward.

qa.q: What did Ramesh train as?
qa.a: He trained as a peer educator.

qa.q: How did Varun feel when Ramesh asked his question?
qa.a: It hit him hard, making him realise with some discomfort that he had only been checking for a no, not for a real yes.

qa.q: What habits did Varun build, and why are they responsible?
qa.a: He now asks out loud, accepts that answers can change, gets tested and carries protection, taking his share of responsibility for safety and consent.

qa.q: How might Varun's past partner see his new approach if she heard about it?
qa.a: She might feel it was a lesson learned late, but may be glad he now takes consent seriously.

grounding: A young man describes learning that consent needs a clear yes and taking responsibility for sexual health.

passage: I'm Anirban, and Saurabh has been my flatmate since first year. Last month his girlfriend stayed over after a party. In the morning I heard them talking in the kitchen, more serious than usual. Later Saurabh told me that when they got back from the party, she'd said she'd had too much to drink and didn't want anything to happen, so he'd made her tea and slept on the floor mat. He looked a bit sheepish. "Is that weird?" he asked. I told him no, that's what you do. She thanked him. They're still together. Last week he brought home a leaflet from the student health clinic about safer sex and left it on our shared shelf. He's never been the type to talk about these things, but he seems to take them seriously.

qa.q: Where did Saurabh sleep that night?
qa.a: He slept on the floor mat.

qa.q: Why might Saurabh have looked sheepish when he asked "Is that weird?"
qa.a: He may have worried that friends would tease him for not pursuing more, even though he felt he did the right thing.

qa.q: What did Saurabh get right in this situation?
qa.a: He respected that she'd had too much to drink and didn't want anything, and he cared for her instead of pressuring her.

qa.q: How might Saurabh's girlfriend feel about his choice?
qa.a: She likely felt safe and respected, which helped build trust in the relationship. 🤍

grounding: A flatmate observes a young man respecting consent when his partner has been drinking and taking sexual health seriously.

passage:
Dear Papa,
I'm writing because when we talk on the phone, we end up arguing. I know you want the best for me. You drove me to every exam, and I'll never forget that.
But I'm twenty now, and I need to make some decisions myself. I want to choose my own internship, even if it pays less. I'd love your advice, just not your final decision.
Also, can we stop the daily 10 pm calls? I'll call every Sunday, and more if something's up. I promise.
Jeevan says his parents took a while too, and now they're closer than ever. I'd like that for us.
I love you. Please don't read this as me pushing you away.
Siddharth

qa.q: How often does Siddharth want to call instead of every day?
qa.a: He wants to call every Sunday, and more if something's up.

qa.q: What does Siddharth's last line reveal about his feelings?
qa.a: It reveals he's worried his father might feel rejected, and he wants to set boundaries while keeping the love between them.

qa.q: What made Siddharth's letter a respectful way to set boundaries?
qa.a: He thanked his father, asked for advice rather than decisions, and offered a clear alternative to the daily calls.

qa.q: How might Papa feel reading this letter?
qa.a: He might feel sad or hurt at first, but also proud of his son's maturity and reassured by the promise of Sunday calls.

grounding: A young man's letter to his father moves from dependence towards an adult partnership with clear boundaries.

passage: You want to know what changed with my parents? I'm Gautam, twenty-one. Until second year of college, my mother packed my bag when I went home and repacked it when I left. I let her. Then I started cooking in my shared flat and realised I liked it. So on my next visit I said, "Ma, let me make dinner." She looked hurt at first. Like I'd taken her job away. My sister Rehana said, "She feels useful when she does things for you." That made sense. So I asked Ma to teach me her dal instead. We cooked together. Now when I visit, I make one meal and she makes one. She tells her friends I cook. She sounds proud.

qa.q: Whose dal recipe did Gautam ask to learn?
qa.a: Gautam asked to learn Ma's dal.

qa.q: Why did Ma look hurt when Gautam offered to cook?
qa.a: She felt her role of caring for Gautam was being taken away; as Rehana said, she feels useful when she does things for Gautam.

qa.q: What made Gautam's solution work?
qa.a: Instead of just taking over, Gautam asked Ma to teach the dal, so she still felt valued while Gautam became more independent.

qa.q: How might Rehana see the change in her brother and mother?
qa.a: She probably feels glad that her insight helped, and sees them relating more like equals now.

grounding: A young adult describes shifting from dependence to a more adult, shared relationship with Gautam's mother.

passage: I'm Gurleen, Indu's older cousin. Indu is twenty-two and just started her first job. Her father used to decide everything for her: her subjects, her college, even her friends. At family dinners he'd speak for her. This Diwali I saw something different. When Chacha said she should move back home to save rent, Indu put down her plate and said calmly, "I've thought about it, Papa. I want to stay in my flat. I'll visit every month." There was a silence. Chachi looked worried. Then Chacha nodded slowly, and asked about her rent. Indu showed him her budget on paper. He looked it over carefully. I don't know how she felt inside, but her hands were steady. Later, they played cards together, laughing.

qa.q: How often did Indu say she would visit?
qa.a: She said she would visit every month.

qa.q: What might Indu's steady hands suggest?
qa.a: They suggest she felt prepared and determined, even if she was nervous, because she had thought it through.

qa.q: What made Indu's way of setting a boundary effective?
qa.a: She spoke calmly, gave a clear plan, and showed her budget, which respected her father while asserting her own choice.

qa.q: How might Chacha feel about Indu's decision?
qa.a: He might feel a little sad to have less control, but also reassured by her careful planning and proud of her.

grounding: A cousin observes a young woman setting a healthy boundary and moving toward an adult partnership with her parents.

passage:
"Preeti! You picked up!"
"Zubin, it's been three months. Of course I picked up."
"I'm sorry. The job's been crazy. I kept meaning to call."
"I know. Me too, with the thesis." She paused. "Honestly, I thought we were drifting."
"We are. That's why I'm calling." He took a breath. "What if we set a thing? Every second Sunday, a call. Even ten minutes."
"That sounds like a meeting."
"A meeting with chai and gossip."
She laughed. "Okay. And if one of us cancels?"
"Then that person sends a voice note with a full update. Punishment."
"Deal."
"And when I come to Pune in May—"
"You're staying at mine. No hotel."
"Deal."

qa.q: How often did Zubin suggest they call?
qa.a: He suggested every second Sunday.

qa.q: What was Preeti feeling before Zubin's call?
qa.a: She was worried they were drifting apart and perhaps a little hurt by the three months of silence.

qa.q: Why is a regular call a good idea for keeping their friendship alive?
qa.a: A fixed small commitment, even ten minutes, makes staying in touch easier than waiting for free time that never comes.

qa.q: How might Zubin feel after the call?
qa.a: He probably feels relieved and happy that Preeti still wants to stay close, and reassured by her offer to host him.

grounding: It shows two young friends making a practical plan to keep their friendship alive despite distance and busy schedules.

passage: When I left for my first job in Hyderabad, I thought my school friendships would last forever on their own. I'm Samir. Disha and I had been best friends since Class 6. For the first year we texted every day. By the second, it was once a month. Then she got engaged, and I found out from a photo online. That stung. I realised I'd stopped asking about her life. I'd send memes, not questions. So I called her, apologised, and asked about the wedding. We talked for two hours. Now we have a shared playlist and add songs every week, and I actually put her birthday in my calendar. I flew back for her wedding. It's not the same as school, but it's real.

qa.q: How did Samir find out Disha got engaged?
qa.a: Samir found out from a photo online.

qa.q: Why did finding out from a photo sting Samir?
qa.a: It made Samir realise how far they had drifted, and that Samir was no longer part of her important moments.

qa.q: What changes helped Samir and Disha stay close?
qa.a: Samir apologised, asked real questions instead of sending memes, and they started small shared habits like a weekly playlist.

qa.q: How might Disha have felt when Samir called and apologised?
qa.a: She may have been relieved and happy that Samir still cared, since they talked for two hours.

grounding: A young adult reflects on letting a close friendship drift across distance and taking steps to sustain it.

passage:
Hostel warden's note, final year:
Karthik and Hrithik were roommates for three years and very close. This year Hrithik moved off campus for an internship, and Karthik seemed low; he mentioned that Hrithik was always "too busy" to reply. I suggested he try something small and concrete rather than waiting. He decided to invite Hrithik for Saturday breakfast at the mess, like old times.
Hrithik came, a bit late and tired. They sat together for an hour, and I heard them laughing. Afterwards, Karthik told me Hrithik had been feeling guilty and overwhelmed, not uninterested.
Follow-up: they now have breakfast every other Saturday. Karthik seems more settled.

qa.q: What did Karthik invite Hrithik for?
qa.a: He invited him for Saturday breakfast at the mess.

qa.q: What had Hrithik been feeling, according to Karthik?

qa.q: Why was the warden's suggestion useful?
qa.a: A small, concrete invitation was easier for a busy friend to accept than waiting for replies, and it led to an honest talk.

qa.q: How might Hrithik see the regular breakfasts?
qa.a: He might feel relieved to have a simple way to stay connected despite his busy internship.

grounding: A warden's note shows young adults sustaining a friendship across new schedules with small regular plans.

passage:
Dear Tushar,
It's been three weeks in Bengaluru. The hostel is fine. The classes are fine. Everything is fine, except I eat dinner alone most nights and scroll through photos from home. Yesterday I heard someone speaking Urdu in the market and nearly cried.
I miss our evenings on the terrace so much it hurts.
But I'm trying. I joined the college book club, even though I only know one person there. We're reading something about mountains. And a girl from my corridor asked if I wanted to go for dosa on Friday. I said yes before I could chicken out.
Write back, okay? Tell me something from home. 🥺
Dilnaz

qa.q: What club did Dilnaz join?
qa.a: Dilnaz joined the college book club.

qa.q: Why did Dilnaz nearly cry in the market?
qa.a: Hearing Urdu reminded Dilnaz of home, and loneliness and nostalgia rose all at once.

passage: You're recording this for the campus radio? Okay. I'm Gopika. When I moved from Thrissur to Delhi for college, I didn't know one person. My roommate went home every weekend. I'd sit in my room, eat biscuits and call Amma for hours. She got worried. Then Uday, a senior from my home state, posted in a group that some of them cook Onam food together every year. I almost didn't go. I was scared I'd be the awkward one. But I went, and someone handed me a coconut to grate. By the end, I had four phone numbers. It wasn't magic. I still feel homesick sometimes. But now I have people to feel homesick with, which is honestly better.

qa.q: What was Gopika handed at the Onam cooking?
qa.a: She was handed a coconut to grate.

qa.q: What helped Gopika build belonging?

qa.q: How might Amma have felt after Gopika found friends?
qa.a: She would likely feel relieved and less worried, hearing her daughter had people around her.

grounding: A young woman describes loneliness after moving to a new city and finding belonging through a shared cultural group.

passage: I'm Kiran, and Urmila joined our office team in Mumbai last month, straight out of college and new to the city. She's polite and works hard, but at lunch she eats at her desk and watches videos. When we invited her for chai, she said, "Maybe later." Last Friday I noticed her staring at a photo of a big family dinner on her phone. I didn't know what to say, so I just asked, "Your family?" She nodded and her eyes went a bit wet. "I've never lived alone before," she said. On Monday I saved her a seat at lunch. She came. She laughed at my terrible joke. On Wednesday she asked if anyone wanted to try the new dosa place. I think she's finding her way in.

passage: The four girls in Room 12 of the working women's hostel had a problem: the bathroom. Payal cleaned it every Sunday; the others forgot. By the third week, she was furious. She left a sticky note: "I'm not your maid." Madhuri, the youngest, took it personally and cried. That evening the warden suggested they sit together. Payal took a breath and said, "I'm sorry about the note. I'm tired of doing it alone." Madhuri said she hadn't known it was a problem because nobody said anything. They made a rota on the fridge, split the cost of cleaning supplies, and agreed to raise things at a weekly ten-minute check-in. It wasn't perfect, but Payal stopped seething on Sundays.

qa.q: What did Payal write on the sticky note?
qa.a: She wrote, "I'm not your maid."

qa.q: Why did Madhuri cry after reading the note?

qa.q: What made the roommates' final solution fair?
qa.a: They talked openly, split chores with a rota, shared supply costs and set up weekly check-ins to raise issues early.

qa.q: How might the warden see the girls' solution?
qa.a: She might be pleased they resolved it themselves with a clear system instead of letting the conflict grow.

grounding: It shows young women in a hostel resolving a chore conflict by talking and sharing work and costs fairly.

passage:
Hi Hafsa,
I'm writing this instead of talking because I get flustered, and I want to say it right.
I've noticed the electricity bill is much higher since the heater came in. I also know you work night shifts, so it's needed. But I'm paying half and I'm hardly home. Could we split it based on use, maybe 60-40, or you cover the heater months?
Also, the kitchen. I know I left dishes last week, and I'm sorry. Can we both wash our own on the same day?
I really like living with you. I don't want small things to become big things.

passage: You want to know how we stopped fighting? I'm Chandrika. Rashmi and I share a two-bedroom flat in Chennai, and for the first three months it was a war. She played music at midnight. I left my laundry on the chair for days. We both paid rent late, and our landlord shouted at both of us. One night she said, "I'm about to move out." That scared me. So we sat on the floor with snacks and wrote down what drove us crazy. It was honestly funny. Hers: my laundry. Mine: her music. We agreed on quiet hours after 11, a laundry deadline, and a shared account for rent. Now we fight maybe once a month, about who ate the last mango.

passage: Selin had been working at a café in Istanbul while finishing university. For months she slept badly, skipped meals and said "fine" when anyone asked. She stopped going to her Friday dance class. Her friend Rafael noticed she hadn't laughed in weeks. One evening he found her sitting in the storeroom, staring at the shelves. "I don't feel anything," she said. "I'm tired all the time and nothing seems worth it." Rafael sat with her. "That sounds heavy. Would you talk to someone? The university has a counsellor." She shrugged, but he helped her book an appointment on his phone right there. The next week she went. She said afterwards it was strange but a relief to say it all out loud.

qa.q: What class did Selin stop going to?
qa.a: She stopped going to her Friday dance class.

qa.q: What does Selin's "I don't feel anything" suggest about her state?
qa.a: It suggests she was deeply exhausted and emotionally numb, and had lost hope, which are warning signs to take seriously.

qa.q: What made Rafael's response helpful?
qa.a: He listened without judging and helped her book a counsellor appointment immediately, turning concern into a concrete step.

qa.q: How might Rafael feel after Selin went to the counsellor?
qa.a: He might feel relieved and hopeful, but also keep checking on her since recovery takes time. 🤍

grounding: It shows a young woman's prolonged exhaustion and hopelessness noticed by a friend who helps her get professional help early.

passage: In the engineering college library, Anand noticed his lab partner Lalremsiami had changed. She used to be the first to answer; now she stared at her screen for an hour without typing. passage:
After dinner at home, Anand looked up from the sofa. "Karthik, why are you checking your phone every five minutes?"
"It's the match, Anand bhaiya. I've got a bit riding on it."
"A bit?"
"Just a small bet. On the app."
"You said that last month. And the month before."
Karthik looked away. "I'm about to win back what I lost."
"How much did you lose?"
Silence. Then, "More than my stipend."
"Karthik."
"I know. I know. Every time I lose, I think the next one will fix it. And when I win, I want to bet more."
"That sounds like a trap."
"It is." His voice cracked. "I don't know how to stop."
Anand sat down beside his younger brother. "Okay. We'll find help. The counselling centre does this. I'll come."
Karthik nodded, and deleted the app while Anand watched.

qa.q: How much had Karthik lost?
qa.a: He had lost more than his stipend.

passage: I didn't think gaming could be a problem until it was. I'm Shreya. In second year, I started playing online after classes. Then through dinner. Then through the night. I told myself I could stop anytime. I skipped my brother Siddharth's birthday call because I was mid-match. That's when I felt sick about it. I tried to quit on my own, but I'd last two days, feel restless, and go back. It was like my brain needed it. Finally I told a college counsellor. She helped me see the loop: stress, play, relief, guilt, more stress. We made a plan with blocked hours and things to do instead, like evening walks with a friend. I still play sometimes. But I choose when.

qa.q: Whose birthday call did Shreya skip?
qa.a: She skipped her brother Siddharth's birthday call.

qa.q: Why did Shreya feel sick after skipping the call?
qa.a: She realised gaming was pushing out the people she loved, which made her see the habit was out of control.

qa.q: How did the counsellor help Shreya exit the loop?
qa.a: She helped her understand the cycle of stress, play, relief and guilt, and plan blocked hours and alternative activities.

qa.q: How might Siddharth feel about Shreya's change?
qa.a: Siddharth may have been hurt by the missed call; now that Shreya chooses when she plays, there may be more room for calls with him.

grounding: A young woman reflects on a gaming dependence loop and how she exited it with professional help.

passage:
College counsellor's note:
Jatin, 21, came in after his friend Gopika urged him to. He said he drinks "a bit" most nights to fall asleep and to cope with stress about exams. Over the last few months he's needed more to feel the same, and he feels anxious and shaky when he skips it. He missed two exams. He was defensive at first, saying "everyone drinks in college." When I asked what he wanted his life to look like in a year, he became quiet and said, "Not like this."
We discussed the cycle of stress, drinking, worse sleep and more stress. I referred him to the campus doctor and a support group. Next steps: weekly sessions. He asked if Gopika could come to the first support meeting.

qa.q: How many exams did Jatin miss?
qa.a: He missed two exams.

qa.q: What does Jatin's "Not like this" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests that under his defensiveness, he was unhappy with where his drinking was taking him and wanted to change.

qa.q: What did the counsellor do that was helpful?
qa.a: The counsellor didn't argue with his defensiveness but asked about his future, explained the cycle, and referred him to a doctor and support group.

qa.q: How might Gopika feel when Jatin asks Gopika to come to the support meeting?
qa.a: Gopika might feel relieved and trusted, glad the urging led Jatin to get help.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a young man recognising an alcohol dependence loop and starting professional help.

passage: Joseph grew up in a small town where everyone expected him to join his uncle's sand-mining business. It paid well. But at twenty, back home from college for the summer, he walked along the river with his friend Pooja and saw how the banks were collapsing. Fishermen complained that the fish were gone. Joseph felt sick. "My uncle's trucks did this," he said. Pooja asked, "So what will you do?" He didn't answer. At dinner, his uncle offered him a manager's job. Everyone looked at him. Joseph's heart pounded. "Thank you, Chachan. But I can't do this work. I want to study environmental science." His uncle's face went hard. His mother looked worried. Later, she squeezed his hand.

qa.q: What job did Joseph's uncle offer him?
qa.a: He offered him a manager's job in the sand-mining business.

qa.q: Why did Joseph's heart pound at dinner?
qa.a: He was about to refuse his family's expectation, knowing it might anger his uncle and upset his family.

qa.q: What helped Joseph find his non-negotiable?
qa.a: Seeing the damaged riverbanks and hearing the fishermen made the cost real, and Pooja's question pushed him to decide.

qa.q: How might Joseph's mother feel about his choice?
qa.a: She seemed worried about the family tension, but her squeezing his hand suggests she supports him quietly.

grounding: It shows a young man choosing his own value of protecting the environment over his family's expectations.

passage: Ulla was twenty and working part-time at a clothing shop in Stockholm. Her friend Ines told her the shop's suppliers used cheap factory labour abroad, with long hours and little safety. Ulla didn't believe it at first. Then she read the reports. She felt ashamed every time she folded a shirt. Her friends said, "Everyone buys from them. What difference does it make?" But Ulla decided she didn't want to earn money that way. She gave notice and found a job at a second-hand shop instead, even though it paid less. Her mother worried about rent. Ulla said, "I'll manage. I need to be able to look at myself." Ines helped her move her things.

qa.q: Where did Ulla find a new job?
qa.a: She found a job at a second-hand shop.

qa.q: Why did Ulla feel ashamed while folding shirts?
qa.a: She felt the shop's success was linked to workers being treated badly, which clashed with her values.

qa.q: What was important about how Ulla made her decision?
qa.a: She checked the facts herself, weighed the cost, and chose based on her values rather than what her friends said.

qa.q: How might Ulla's mother see her decision?
qa.a: She might feel worried about money but also respect her daughter's integrity.

grounding: It shows a young woman defining a personal value about fair work and acting on it despite peers' views.

passage: At the start of her first job at an accounting firm in Gurugram, Simran was asked by her manager to adjust some numbers "just a little" so a client's report looked better. Her colleague Aditi shrugged. "It happens. Don't make it a big deal." Simran went home and couldn't sleep. Her family needed her salary. But she kept thinking of her grandfather, who used to say, "Your name is all you really own." The next morning she went to her manager. "I'm not comfortable changing those figures. Can we show the real numbers and explain them?" He frowned but didn't push. Aditi later told her, quietly, "I wish I'd said that." Simran realised she'd drawn her first real line.

qa.q: What did Simran's grandfather use to say?
qa.a: He used to say, "Your name is all you really own."

qa.q: Why couldn't Simran sleep that night?
qa.a: She was torn between her family needing her salary and her discomfort at doing something dishonest.

qa.q: What made Simran's way of refusing effective?
qa.a: She spoke calmly, stated her discomfort and offered an honest alternative, which made it harder for the manager to push.

qa.q: How might Aditi feel after Simran spoke up?
qa.a: She seems to regret her own silence, and may feel encouraged to stand firmer next time.

grounding: It shows a young woman defining honesty as a non-negotiable value at her first job despite pressure.

passage:
Dear Darshan,
You asked how I got through failing my driving test twice. Honestly? The first time I went home and called myself useless all evening. The second time I didn't sleep. I kept replaying every mistake.
Then my aunt asked me, "Would you talk to a friend like that?" No way. So I tried something. I wrote down what went wrong: I rushed the parking, I panicked at the roundabout. And then what I'd practise: slow parking, three roundabouts every Sunday.
It felt weird, like being my own coach instead of my own critic.
I passed the third time. I still made a mistake, but I didn't spiral.
You'll get your exam next time too. Be kind to yourself.
Parul

qa.q: How many times did Parul fail the driving test?
qa.a: Parul failed it twice.

qa.q: How did Parul feel after the first failure?
qa.a: Parul felt useless and harshly self-critical all evening, which made things feel worse.

qa.q: What made Parul's new approach work?
qa.a: Parul named specific mistakes and planned practice instead of self-attack, which kept Parul accountable without spiralling.

qa.q: If you were Darshan, how might this letter help you?
qa.a: It shows that failing doesn't mean you're useless, and gives a simple method to learn from mistakes kindly.

grounding: A young adult's letter describes replacing harsh self-criticism with accountable, supportive self-talk after failure.

passage: You're asking how I handle mistakes now? I'm Pallavi. Last year I messed up a major presentation at my internship. I forgot half my points, froze, and my manager had to take over. I went to the washroom and told myself I was stupid, that I'd never be good enough. For days I barely spoke. Then my friend Darshan, over chai, asked me what I'd tell a junior who froze like that. I said, "That it happens. That she should practise more and it's not the end." He just raised his eyebrows. I laughed, and then cried a little. Now when I make a mistake, I say to myself: "Okay. What happened? What will I do differently?" I still feel bad. But I don't hate myself anymore.

qa.q: Who asked Pallavi what she would tell a junior?
qa.a: Her friend Darshan asked her, over chai.

qa.q: Why did Pallavi laugh and then cry a little?
qa.a: She felt amused and sad at once, realising how much kinder she was to others than to herself.

qa.q: What self-talk does Pallavi use now, and why does it help?
qa.a: She asks what happened and what she'll do differently, which keeps her responsible without tearing herself down.

qa.q: How might Pallavi's manager see her now?
qa.a: The manager may notice she recovers faster from mistakes and learns from them.

grounding: A young woman describes moving from harsh self-criticism to supportive self-talk after failing at work.

passage: I'm Himani, Chetan's classmate in the MBA programme. When he didn't make it to the final round of the placement interviews, he went very quiet. That evening, in the common room, I heard him say to himself, "You're such an idiot. You always mess up." He said it more than once. The next day he skipped class. On Friday, I saw him sitting with a notebook in the library, writing. I peeked, and he'd written: "Didn't prepare for case questions. Next time: practise with a friend twice a week." He asked me if I wanted to be that friend. I said yes. I don't know what changed in him, but he seemed calmer after that, and he stopped calling himself names out loud.

qa.q: What did Chetan write in his notebook?
qa.a: He wrote, "Didn't prepare for case questions. Next time: practise with a friend twice a week."

qa.q: What does Chetan calling himself an idiot suggest about his feelings?
qa.a: It suggests he felt ashamed and angry at himself, and was being very harsh after the failure.

qa.q: What changed in how Chetan handled his failure?
qa.a: He moved from name-calling to writing a clear, practical plan, which kept him accountable without tearing himself down.

qa.q: How might Himani feel being asked to be his practice partner?
qa.a: Himani might feel glad and trusted, happy to support Chetan as he recovers.

grounding: A classmate observes a young man replacing harsh self-criticism with accountable planning after failure.
